text: Palaces sinking gracefully into the lagoon, one lit window at a time. Venice in December: fog, bells, and nobody here but the pigeons and the spies.
Maschere Ca' Rosa: masks in the window, gold, black, white, and one long-nosed plague doctor. Tonight, the whole city will be wearing somebody else's face.
Closed. A card in the door: "Back at seven. Or eight. Venice."
A lamp coming on in the fog. Very romantic. I'm in Venice with a goose and a seventy-year-old opera singer. Also very romantic.
A gondola, black as a piano, with a red velvet seat and a steel comb on the prow. The gondolier is asleep on the crate beside it.
I could row it myself. I could also fall in. Better to wake the gondolier.
Hey! Fifty thousand lire first, signore. Then you get in. That is the Venetian way.
A paper cone of corn, dropped on the stones. Somebody fed the pigeons, and the pigeons fed on somebody.
Corn. Every bird in Venice wants this. I know one in particular.
Madame Novak, on a bench in the fog in a fur coat, as if Venice had been arranged around her. It probably was.
I do not feed pigeons, darling. I have seen what they do to statues.
Toni the gondolier: striped jersey, straw boater, and the outraged look of a man who has just been attacked by a goose.
A gondolier, asleep on a crate of glass with his boater over his eyes. His snores are keeping the fog away.
Excuse me? Signore?
Zzz... fifty thousand lire... zzz... one more song... zzz...
Asleep. Deeply. I'd need a brass band to wake him. Or something louder.
Murano! Hop in, signore. The goose sits at the front. She is ballast.
Murano? At this time? Fifty thousand lire. For the goose, another fifty. She looks heavy.
No! No corn! Keep the corn away from me!
Back into the maze of alleys. Venice has four hundred bridges and I have crossed three hundred of them looking for this bench.
There you are, darling. I have been sitting on this bench since four. The pigeons have proposed twice.
Madame Novak. You got my telegram.

I got your telegram, your postcard and your goose feathers. And I heard every word of that telephone call through my little tulip. The call to Istanbul did not come from London, darling. It came from here. The Hotel Danieli, room forty-one.
The London buyer is in Venice?
Collecting in person. Vasko is not handing over the aeroplane. He is handing over the launch codes, on microfilm, hidden inside a Murano glass swan.
And the swan is the centrepiece at the Contessa Lucrezia's masked ball tonight. At midnight, she gives it as a gift to her guest from London. Very elegant. Very Venetian. Very criminal.
Then we need a swan of our own.
The glassblower who made it is Maestro Bepi, on Murano. Across the lagoon. You will need a boat, darling. And that one comes with a gondolier, although at the moment he is asleep.
Every gondolier in Venice is asleep in December, darling. You must wake him up. Gently. Or not.
He wants fifty thousand lire. I have two Turkish coins and a false moustache.
Leave it to me.
Signor gondolier. Fifty thousand lire, and fifty for the goose. And fifty to forget our faces.
Grazie, signora! What faces?
Madame Novak, I'll pay you back.
Nonsense, darling. Expenses. I shall send the bill to my son.
Go to Murano. I shall find us some masks and meet you at the Contessa's water gate at nine.
Go, darling. Murano. And don't let the Maestro sell you a chandelier.
A little corn on the hat. For luck.
Come on, Colonel. Dinner is served.
Mamma mia! A goose! A goose is eating my hat!
Via! Go away! Shoo! I am a gondolier, not a picnic!
Sorry to wake you. I need to get to Murano.
Ahh, the furnace. I warm my hands, signore. Take your time. I am paid by the hour. By the signora.
Murano: every glass chandelier in the world was born on this island. It is also the hottest room in Venice in December.
The furnace, white-hot at the heart. Twelve hundred degrees. The goose is keeping a respectful distance for once.
Touch my furnace and you will be a very small glass man.
Vases, bowls and bottles in every colour of a boiled sweet. One of them is shaped like a Pope. I think by accident.
Three glass swans on a shelf. The first two are perfect. The third one has a slight droop, like a swan on a Monday.
Put that down! Those are for the Queen of Denmark. Well, one is. The droopy one is for my mother-in-law.
Long iron blowpipes in a rack. You put one end in the fire and the other in your mouth, and hope you don't get them mixed up.
Fornace Bepi, since 1921. Maestro Bepi looks as if he has been here since 1921 personally.
Bills, spiked on a nail by the door. The one on top has UNPAID stamped on it in red, three times.
To Colonel Vasko: one swan, hollow, with a cork in the tail. Three million lire. Third reminder.
Vasko ordered the swan, and never paid for it. That sounds like Vasko.
Maestro Bepi: eighty years old, eyebrows singed off in 1950 and never grown back, and arms like a blacksmith.
Take it away. Every time I look at it, it looks back.
Toni, in his vest, very happy to be missing the Contessa's party.
Toni, warming his hands at the furnace and humming O Sole Mio. Badly.
Remember: O Sole Mio. Eleven times. And smile. She tips if you smile.
Take your time, signore. I am in no hurry. Tonight I must sing at the Contessa's ball. I hate the Contessa's ball.
Why?
She makes me sing O Sole Mio. Eleven times. It is a song from Naples! I am Venetian! It is like asking a Scotsman to sing in Welsh!
Not without a swan of my own.
I have a swan. Now I need a way into the ball. Toni is supposed to be singing at it.
Go. Take your goose. Both of them.
Closed! The shop is closed. The furnace is never closed, but the shop is closed.
Maestro, I need a glass swan. The same as the one you made for the Contessa's ball.
The same? The SAME? Bepi does not make the same. Every swan of Bepi is unique. Like a snowflake. Like a fingerprint. Like my mother-in-law.
Besides, that swan was not for the Contessa. A foreign colonel ordered it. Hollow, with a little cork in the tail. What does a man put in a swan? I did not ask.
No copies. No discounts. No geese in the workshop.
...No geese!
The foreign colonel who ordered that swan. Did he ever pay you?
Pay? PAY? Three reminders I send! Three! The Colonel says: "It is an honour for you to work for me." An honour does not pay for gas, signore!
What if I told you that swan is going to make him fifty million dollars tonight? Unless somebody swaps it for another one.
...For the Colonel, I make an exception. For the Colonel, I make a swan he will never forget.
But my assistant has gone home. He has a cold. You will work the bellows. When I say blow, you blow.
The gather. Now, the body. Blow! Gently!
Too gently! It is a swan, not a soap bubble!
Too hard! Now it is a swan that has eaten a swan!
The goose blows better than my assistant. Do not tell him.
Now the neck. I pull, you turn the pipe. Slowly, slowly...
Slowly! Not backwards!
Bless you. And bless the neck, because now it has a bend in it.
No. Nothing I make is meant to droop. Except my mother-in-law's swan.
Finished. Cooled with magic, and a bucket.
It is... a goose. A goose that wishes it were a swan. Like my brother-in-law.
It's perfect. In a dark ballroom, after three glasses of prosecco, nobody will know the difference.
Everybody will know the difference. But the Colonel will be embarrassed, and that, signore, is priceless.
Toni. How would you like the night off?
The night off? From the Contessa? From O Sole Mio?
I go to the ball in your place. You row, and you wait at the water gate. I sing.
Signore, you are an angel. An angel with a goose. Take the jersey! Take the hat! Take the song!
Bellissimo! You look like a real gondolier. Only more nervous.
Anything else I should know?
O Sole Mio. Eleven times. And smile. She tips if you smile.
The Grand Canal at night, through Gothic windows five hundred years old. Out there, Toni and the Colonel are waiting in the gondola. One of them is eating a mask.
A string quartet playing a waltz. The cellist has fallen asleep, and the other three are covering for him.
My swan, under the dome. It's staring at the guests. The guests are staring back. Nobody has said anything yet.
The swan, on a marble plinth under a glass dome, lit like a jewel in a museum. Kolar is standing next to it like a museum guard who has been told there will be no pay rise.
Step away from the swan, gondolier. Nobody touches the swan until midnight.
I can't walk out with it under my arm. I need to leave something in its place.
Step away from the swan, gondolier. And take your... goose with you.
A silver urn, a row of teacups, and a card: Prosecco, Tè. Every guest in the room is drinking prosecco. One cup of tea has been poured.
Contessa Lucrezia: a gold mask, violet silk, a palazzo on the Grand Canal and a laugh you could hear in Padua.
Gondolier! You sing again at midnight. And at midnight, I give the swan to my guest from London. A little gift. He has paid for it already.
Which guest is from London, Contessa?
Darling, it is a masked ball. Nobody is from anywhere.
Madame Novak, waltzing with Kolar and leading. He hasn't noticed.
Madame Novak in a golden mask. Somehow she is still the most recognisable person in the room.
Kolar, waltzing, counting under his breath: one two three, one two three.
A tall man in a black mask, standing by the swan with his hands behind his back. The mask doesn't help. It's Kolar.
One two three, one two three... Not now, gondolier!
Gondolier. Have we met?
Everybody in Venice has met a gondolier, signore.
...True.
A waiter with a tray of prosecco, gliding through the crowd like a swan. A real one.
A plague doctor: black hat, black cloak, and a long white beak. He is stirring a cup of tea. Very. Loudly.
The only man in Venice drinking tea at a ball. "Very English," Leyla said. "He stirs his tea very loudly."
Buonasera, dottore.
He isn't going to talk. He's going to stir that tea until it confesses.
A small white mask, a huge white hat, and a Texan accent you could hear from Houston. Mr Hollis, incognito.
Howdy, gondola man! Don't tell anybody, but I'm in disguise. Lost out on that invisible airplane, so I'm buying me a palazzo. Sinks a little, but so does Houston.
A white bauta mask with a banker's chin underneath it. Herr Brunner of Zürich.
I am not here. If you see me, you did not. If I see you, I shall invoice you.
Not without the swan.
Not yet. I need to know who the London buyer is. Somebody in this room.
Gondolier! You are late! Where is Toni?
Toni has a cold, Contessa. I'm his cousin. Giacomo.
Giacomo. You will sing. Now.
O sole mio... sta nfronte a te...
Terrible. Wonderful. Toni sings it exactly the same. Again at midnight!
Volare, oh oh... cantare, oh oh oh oh...
That is not O Sole Mio. But the Americans are clapping. Again at midnight! The right one!
God save our gracious Queen...
What a strange Venetian song. The man in the beak has stopped stirring his tea. Again at midnight!
Darling. You were magnificent. Nobody will ever forget it, which is the problem.
Somewhere in this room is the swan. And somewhere in this room is the man from London.
Not now, darling. The Captain is about to step on my foot for the ninth time.
Find the swan first, darling. Then tell me who I have to dance with.
Kolar is guarding the swan. I need him somewhere else for five minutes.
Five minutes? Darling, I could keep a man busy for five years. I did, twice.
Captain. You look like a man who waltzes beautifully.
I... I am on duty, madame.
So is the orchestra, and look at them.
...One dance.
More prosecco, gondolier? No. Gondoliers do not drink on duty. Only on land.
Prosecco, signore? No, you are staff. Look busy, then.
Is anyone here drinking tea?
Tea? At a ball? Only one guest has asked for tea all night. That one, in the beak. Four sugars, and he stirs it like he is angry with it.
"Very English. He stirs his tea very loudly." Leyla, in Istanbul, about the man on the telephone.
One swan out. One goose in.
Say, is that swan lookin' at me funny?
Now: which of these masks is the man from London?
Midnight! Midnight, my darlings! And now, the moment we have all been waiting for!
For my guest from London, a little gift from Venice: a swan of Murano glass!
Behold!
Well, I'll be. That ain't a swan. That's a goose.
...It is modern art!
Captain. The gondolier.
The gondolier... the baker... the waiter... HARROW!
Buonanotte, everybody! Same time next year!
There you are, darling. I took a water taxi. It had a heater.
I rowed across Venice with the Karvonian army behind me.
I know, darling. You woke up the whole city. The Patriarch of Venice has complained.
The Rialto at dawn, pink and gold, with the shutters still down on every shop. Four hundred years of people meeting here to do business they shouldn't.
The fish market isn't open yet. The gulls are already queueing.
Madame Novak, up all night and still looking better than me.
Well, darling? Let us see what a swan keeps in its tail.
One swan. With a cork in its tail.
And inside... a roll of microfilm. Tiny. Clever. Launch codes, darling. For every Nightglass Vasko will ever build.
I believe that belongs to me. I did pay for it.
Good morning, Mother.
...Rupert?
Control.
Hello, Harrow. You've had a busy week. The train, the mountain, Istanbul, and now my swan.
Rupert Novak, what on earth do you think you are doing?
Buying an aeroplane, Mother. Well, the codes for one. Then selling them to the Americans for twice the price. Have you seen what the Service pays in pensions?
I sent you to the best schools in England!
And that, Mother, is where I learned it.
He was always a difficult boy.
The film, Harrow.
You will have to shoot your mother first, Rupert.
Don't be dramatic, Mother.
...Very well. Keep the film. Keep the swan. Keep the goose. Somebody should.
But you won't keep much else, Harrow. I'm afraid this is where your career ends.
What did he mean by that?
With Rupert, darling, it always means paperwork.
Corn on a sleeping gondolier's hat. The Colonel would do the rest.
The gondolier is fast asleep. Something on the quay by the lamp might get a certain bird interested in him.
Fifty thousand lire. Madame Novak has never let me pay for anything.
The gondola is waiting. Murano.
Maestro Bepi might change his mind about copies if he saw that unpaid bill again.
Bepi won't copy the swan. There are bills on a nail by the door.
Toni has to sing at the Contessa's ball tonight, and he hates it.
Back to the gondola, through the door on the right.
The swan is on the plinth in the middle of the room. I should take a closer look.
Kolar won't leave the swan. But Madame Novak could make any man leave anything.
Kolar is dancing. Bepi's swan goes on the plinth, now.
The London buyer "stirs his tea very loudly". The waiter would know who asked for tea.
Out through the water gate, before midnight.
Madame Novak is waiting. Show her the swan.
Nothing special.
That won't work.
I don't think so.
Not a chance.
That doesn't help here.
Those two don't go together.
Sorry, Toni! I'll bring her back!
After him! He is only a gondolier!
Mind your heads! Gondola coming through!
How is a gondolier so fast?
Fear, mostly!
Under the Rialto, Kolar's launch meets a barge full of cabbages coming the other way. The cabbages win.
Jack spends the rest of the night under a tarpaulin in the fish market, with a glass swan and a goose. At dawn he goes to meet Madame Novak.
In Istanbul, Nightglass was sold for fifty million dollars to a bidder on the telephone, who asked for the goose as well. By name. Madame Novak's tulip was listening.
Jack left Istanbul on a freighter full of hazelnuts, with a goose who ate a great many of them. The freighter was going to Venice. So, it turns out, was the buyer.
Fog on the canals, bells in the fog, and a masked ball tonight at the Palazzo Ca' Rosa.
In a basement in Whitehall a telex machine begins to chatter. The same message goes to every British embassy, consulate and border post in Europe.
HARROW, JACK. AGENT. NOW TRAITOR. DETAIN ON SIGHT.  ALSO ONE GOOSE, WHITE, ANSWERS TO "COLONEL". ALSO TRAITOR.
Wanted.
Chapter Seven: The Wall.
A paper cone of corn, bought by a tourist for the pigeons of Venice and abandoned when the pigeons got too friendly.
FORNACE BEPI. To Col. Vasko: one swan, hollow, with a cork in the tail. Three million lire. THIRD REMINDER. The word "third" is underlined four times.
Maestro Bepi's swan, made with my help. Its neck has sagged, its beak has thickened, and it looks at you like it wants your sandwich. It is a goose.
The real swan: elegant, flawless, and heavier than it looks. There's a little cork in its tail.
Half an hour across black water in the fog. Toni sings the whole way. The goose sits in the prow like a figurehead, and hisses at every passing vaporetto.
Palazzo Ca' Rosa, every window blazing. Gondolas nose up to the water gate, and masked guests step out in silk and feathers. One gondolier, new to the job, rams the steps.
Madame Novak is waiting in a golden mask, with a second mask for the goose. The footman looks at the goose, and at the mask, and says nothing. The goose stays in the gondola with Toni.
